scene-u01-pnew41-66.text: KP02 gives the first complete example with LeNet.

steps.label: KP01 · 1/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Four things first! First: explain why arranging an image into one vector for a fully connected layer loses which pixels are neighbours. Second: on a small image, compute a few numbers of a feature map by hand with a small kernel.

steps.label: KP01 · 1/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Four things first! First: explain why arranging an image into one vector for a fully connected layer loses which pixels are neighbours. Second: on a small image, compute a few numbers of a feature map by hand with a small kernel.

steps.label: KP01 · 1/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Third: count the weights of three wirings, fully connected, neighbours only, and neighbours with shared weights, and say which part each of the two restrictions removes.

steps.label: KP01 · 1/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: Fourth: explain with a small example how the feature map moves when the input shifts, and tell moving with the input from not changing at all. After reading, check yourself against these four.

steps.label: KP01 · 2/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Meet the symbols! H and W are the height and width of the image, the numbers of rows and columns. I at p, q is the pixel value at row p and column q. K at m, n is the weight of the kernel at row m and column n; the kernel has size k by k, with k its side length.

steps.label: KP01 · 2/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Meet the symbols! H and W are the height and width of the image, the numbers of rows and columns. I at p, q is the pixel value at row p and column q. K at m, n is the weight of the kernel at row m and column n; the kernel has size k by k, with k its side length.

steps.label: KP01 · 2/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: s at i, j is the value of the feature map at the output position i, j. m and n are the summation indices that sweep the cells of the kernel. In 1-D, x, w and s are the input, kernel and output.

steps.label: KP01 · 2/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: The star is the sliding multiply-and-add of Section 2, named formally in KP04. Indices start at zero, and the number of parameters never includes biases; this is an added convention.

steps.label: KP01 · 3/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: How to hand over an image? A gray-scale image is an H by W grid of cells; every cell is a pixel that stores one brightness number. The edges and textures in an image are local patterns made of brightness differences between neighbouring pixels, so who is next to whom is among the most important information of an image.

steps.label: KP01 · 3/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: How to hand over an image? A gray-scale image is an H by W grid of cells; every cell is a pixel that stores one brightness number. The edges and textures in an image are local patterns made of brightness differences between neighbouring pixels, so who is next to whom is among the most important information of an image.

steps.label: KP01 · 3/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: The fully connected layer of Week 2 needs a vector as input: every output is connected to every input, and each connection has its own weight.

steps.label: KP01 · 3/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: An image is a grid and a fully connected layer wants a vector, so the shapes do not match. What is the most direct way to hand the image over?

steps.label: KP01 · 4/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Line it up as a vector! Putting the cells row after row into a vector of length H W is called flattening. Flattening throws away no number.

steps.label: KP01 · 4/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Line it up as a vector! Putting the cells row after row into a vector of length H W is called flattening. Flattening throws away no number.

steps.label: KP01 · 4/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: After flattening a four by four image, the pixel at row p and column q lands at position four p plus q. This is an added calculation.

steps.label: KP01 · 4/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: The number on each cell in the figure is its position in the strip: row zero is zero to three, row one is four to seven, and so on.

steps.label: KP01 · 5/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Neighbours torn apart? First look at the image: the orange cell five has the blue cells one, nine, four and six above, below, left and right.

steps.label: KP01 · 5/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Neighbours torn apart? First look at the image: the orange cell five has the blue cells one, nine, four and six above, below, left and right.

steps.label: KP01 · 5/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Then the strip after flattening: the left-right neighbours four and six still touch five, but the up-down neighbours one and nine are four cells away on each side.

steps.label: KP01 · 5/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: Finally the red cell three: in the image it is at the right end of row zero, far from cell four, but in the strip it is next to cell four. The neighbour relation has been rewritten.

steps.label: KP01 · 6/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Does reordering matter? Flattening itself drops no number; the problem lies in the fully connected layer, which treats every input position alike.

steps.label: KP01 · 6/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Does reordering matter? Flattening itself drops no number; the problem lies in the fully connected layer, which treats every input position alike.

steps.label: KP01 · 6/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Reorder the positions of the vector in any way and reorder the weights with them, and the result is exactly the same. This is an added observation.

steps.label: KP01 · 6/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: So for it the fact that cells five and nine are vertical neighbours simply does not exist. Local patterns can only be learned the hard way, from lots of data.

steps.label: KP01 · 7/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: What are the two costs? Cost one: local patterns can only be learned from lots of data. The same edge at different positions needs different weights, learned once each.

steps.label: KP01 · 7/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: What are the two costs? Cost one: local patterns can only be learned from lots of data. The same edge at different positions needs different weights, learned once each.

steps.label: KP01 · 7/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Cost two: the number of weights is the number of inputs times the number of outputs, which is huge for large images.

steps.label: KP01 · 7/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: A common error: thinking that a flattened MLP surely cannot tell handwritten digits apart. It can, but it has many weights to learn and learns local patterns the hard way.

steps.label: KP01 · 8/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Lay the small kernel on! Another way is not to flatten, and to compute directly on the original grid. Prepare a small set of weights arranged in a k by k grid, called a kernel, or a filter.

steps.label: KP01 · 8/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Lay the small kernel on! Another way is not to flatten, and to compute directly on the original grid. Prepare a small set of weights arranged in a k by k grid, called a kernel, or a filter.

steps.label: KP01 · 8/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Lay the kernel on a small patch of the image, multiply the aligned cells and add them all up: one number.

steps.label: KP01 · 8/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: Move the kernel one cell right or down each time and compute again. These numbers, arranged by position, form a new grid called the feature map.

steps.label: KP01 · 9/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: How to read the formula? When the top-left corner of the kernel aligns with image position i, j, the output is s at i, j equal to the sum over m and n of I at i plus m, j plus n times K at m, n.

steps.label: KP01 · 9/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: How to read the formula? When the top-left corner of the kernel aligns with image position i, j, the output is s at i, j equal to the sum over m and n of I at i plus m, j plus n times K at m, n.

steps.label: KP01 · 9/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: The summation indices m and n only sweep each cell of the kernel and have nothing to do with the output position i, j; the pixel multiplied is row i plus m, column j plus n.

steps.label: KP01 · 9/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: The kernel must lie completely inside the image; this kind of output is called a valid output. This formula gets its formal name in KP04 and is compared with the textbook form there.

steps.label: KP01 · 10/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: How many outputs? The kernel must lie completely inside the image, so its top-left corner can stand at five minus three plus one, that is three, positions in each direction.

steps.label: KP01 · 10/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: How many outputs? The kernel must lie completely inside the image, so its top-left corner can stand at five minus three plus one, that is three, positions in each direction.

steps.label: KP01 · 10/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: The blue cells in the figure are the places where the top-left corner can stand, nine in the three by three block.

steps.label: KP01 · 10/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: Each position yields one number, so the feature map is three by three, smaller than the five by five image.

steps.label: KP01 · 11/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Compute s[0,0] first! The main example is a five by five checkerboard image: row p, column q is one when p plus q is even and zero otherwise. The kernel has ones at its four corners and its centre and zeros elsewhere.

steps.label: KP01 · 11/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Compute s[0,0] first! The main example is a five by five checkerboard image: row p, column q is one when p plus q is even and zero otherwise. The kernel has ones at its four corners and its centre and zeros elsewhere.

steps.label: KP01 · 11/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: First look at the framed three by three window at the top left, then at the kernel: the five ones of the kernel cover ones of the image.

steps.label: KP01 · 11/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: Of the nine products only the five where the kernel is one are non-zero, so s at 0, 0 equals I at 0,0 plus I at 0,2 plus I at 1,1 plus I at 2,0 plus I at 2,2, equal to five.

steps.label: KP01 · 12/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Slide one cell right! Slide the window one cell right: now all five ones of the kernel fall on zeros of the image.

steps.label: KP01 · 12/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Slide one cell right! Slide the window one cell right: now all five ones of the kernel fall on zeros of the image.

steps.label: KP01 · 12/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Every one of the nine products is zero, so s at 0, 1 equals zero.

steps.label: KP01 · 12/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: The kernel acts like a pattern detector: when the pattern in the window matches the kernel the output is largest, otherwise it is small.

steps.label: KP01 · 13/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: What does the whole map look like? Computing all nine positions, the three rows of the feature map are five, zero, five; zero, five, zero; five, zero, five.

steps.label: KP01 · 13/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: What does the whole map look like? Computing all nine positions, the three rows of the feature map are five, zero, five; zero, five, zero; five, zero, five.

steps.label: KP01 · 13/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Five appears at the four corners and the centre, the positions where the window pattern matches the kernel.

steps.label: KP01 · 13/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: This is the feature map that the small kernel slides out on the checkerboard. It was recomputed: the numbers are generated and checked by a program.

steps.label: KP01 · 14/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: What is it called? A network that uses this operation as its main component is called a convolutional neural network, and a layer that performs it is a convolutional layer. The kernel is also called a filter, and the grid it produces is the feature map.

steps.label: KP01 · 14/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: What is it called? A network that uses this operation as its main component is called a convolutional neural network, and a layer that performs it is a convolutional layer. The kernel is also called a filter, and the grid it produces is the feature map.

steps.label: KP01 · 14/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Remember the terms first: kernel, feature map, convolutional layer, convolutional neural network.

steps.label: KP01 · 14/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: Compared with a fully connected layer, how much does it save? The next section counts it for the same task.

steps.label: KP01 · 15/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Fix the task first! For a fair comparison, fix the same task: the input is a four by four image and the output is also four by four, with one output for every pixel position. This is called a same-size output.

steps.label: KP01 · 15/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Fix the task first! For a fair comparison, fix the same task: the input is a four by four image and the output is also four by four, with one output for every pixel position. This is called a same-size output.

steps.label: KP01 · 15/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: The window of Section 2 aligns by its top-left corner and the output is smaller than the input. To make the output as large as the input, here the three by three window of each output is centred at its own position.

steps.label: KP01 · 15/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: A window near the border partly lies outside the image, and that part is not wired. This is an added setting; KP07 covers how to fill values at the border.

steps.label: KP01 · 16/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: How many weights, fully connected? The first wiring is fully connected: every output connects to all sixteen pixels.

steps.label: KP01 · 16/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: How many weights, fully connected? The first wiring is fully connected: every output connects to all sixteen pixels.

steps.label: KP01 · 16/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Sixteen outputs, each connected to sixteen pixels, make sixteen times sixteen, equal to two hundred fifty-six connections.

steps.label: KP01 · 16/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: Every connection has its own weight, so there are two hundred fifty-six weights. A connection is one path in which an input pixel feeds one output.

steps.label: KP01 · 17/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Neighbours only? The second wiring: every output connects only to the pixels that really exist in its three by three window.

steps.label: KP01 · 17/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Neighbours only? The second wiring: every output connects only to the pixels that really exist in its three by three window.

steps.label: KP01 · 17/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: The four corners connect four pixels each, the other eight border positions six each, and the four middle ones nine each.

steps.label: KP01 · 17/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: In all sixteen plus forty-eight plus thirty-six, equal to one hundred connections. Each still has its own weight, so there are one hundred weights. This is sparse connectivity.

steps.label: KP01 · 18/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: How many after sharing? The third wiring: neighbours only, and all outputs share one three by three kernel.

steps.label: KP01 · 18/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: How many after sharing? The third wiring: neighbours only, and all outputs share one three by three kernel.

steps.label: KP01 · 18/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: There are still one hundred connections, but only nine different numbers, so there are only nine weights.

steps.label: KP01 · 18/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: A common error is to confuse the number of connections with the number of weights. After sharing, there are still one hundred connections; they just share nine numbers.

steps.label: KP01 · 19/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: 256 → 100 → 9! First the top red bar: the fully connected layer has two hundred fifty-six weights.

steps.label: KP01 · 19/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: 256 → 100 → 9! First the top red bar: the fully connected layer has two hundred fifty-six weights.

steps.label: KP01 · 19/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Down to the first arrow: each output connects only to a small neighbouring patch and every other connection is absent, called sparse connectivity, cutting to one hundred. Then the second arrow: all positions use the same set of kernel weights, called parameter sharing, cutting to nine.

steps.label: KP01 · 19/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: A convolutional layer is just a fully connected layer with these two restrictions, not a different mathematics. The horizontal axis is the number of different weights, and all three bars are for the same four by four input, four by four output task.

steps.label: KP01 · 20/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: We build in an assumption! These two restrictions are also assumptions built into the model before seeing any data. Such an assumption is called an inductive bias, which can be seen as a very strong prior.

steps.label: KP01 · 20/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: We build in an assumption! These two restrictions are also assumptions built into the model before seeing any data. Such an assumption is called an inductive bias, which can be seen as a very strong prior.

steps.label: KP01 · 20/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Sparse connectivity assumes that useful patterns are local; parameter sharing assumes that the same pattern may appear at any position with the same meaning.

steps.label: KP01 · 20/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: For photos both assumptions roughly hold, so the model can learn with fewer weights. Fewer weights also reduce the overfitting risk discussed in Week 4.

steps.label: KP01 · 21/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: What if the image is big? The gap is larger for bigger images. A 28 by 28 gray-scale handwritten digit connected to 512 hidden units needs 784 times 512, equal to 401,408 weights in a fully connected layer.

steps.label: KP01 · 21/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: What if the image is big? The gap is larger for bigger images. A 28 by 28 gray-scale handwritten digit connected to 512 hidden units needs 784 times 512, equal to 401,408 weights in a fully connected layer.

steps.label: KP01 · 21/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: A 224 by 224 colour photo has three numbers, red, green and blue, per pixel, 150,528 numbers in all; connecting it to 512 units takes 77,070,336 weights.

steps.label: KP01 · 21/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: With 64 kernels of size 3 by 3 by 3, the last 3 matching the three colour numbers of each pixel, only 64 times 27, equal to 1,728 weights are needed, and this number does not depend on the image size.

steps.label: KP01 · 22/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Connections = weights? The two layers above have different output sizes, so the two numbers should not be divided directly. This is an added caution.

steps.label: KP01 · 22/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Connections = weights? The two layers above have different output sizes, so the two numbers should not be divided directly. This is an added caution.

steps.label: KP01 · 22/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: The fair same-size comparison is the four by four example above: 256, 100 and 9.

steps.label: KP01 · 22/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: The details of many kernels and colour channels are left to KP07.

steps.label: KP01 · 23/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Switch to 1-D! Use the simplest 1-D example: the signal x sits on a row of six cells, three non-zero values two, one, three and the rest zero; the kernel is w equal to four, five.

steps.label: KP01 · 23/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Switch to 1-D! Use the simplest 1-D example: the signal x sits on a row of six cells, three non-zero values two, one, three and the rest zero; the kernel is w equal to four, five.

steps.label: KP01 · 23/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: The 1-D sliding multiply-add is s at t equal to x at t times w at 0 plus x at t plus one times w at 1. This is an added form.

steps.label: KP01 · 23/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: Indices start at zero, and the kernel moves one cell at a time.

steps.label: KP01 · 24/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Compute the output! The input x is zero, two, one, three, zero, zero and the kernel is four, five. The output s is ten, thirteen, nineteen, twelve, zero.

steps.label: KP01 · 24/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Compute the output! The input x is zero, two, one, three, zero, zero and the kernel is four, five. The output s is ten, thirteen, nineteen, twelve, zero.

steps.label: KP01 · 24/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: For example s at 1 equals two times four plus one times five, equal to thirteen.

steps.label: KP01 · 24/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: Cell by cell: s at 0 is zero times four plus two times five, ten; s at 2 is one times four plus three times five, nineteen; s at 3 is three times four plus zero times five, twelve; the last cell is zero.

steps.label: KP01 · 25/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: What if we shift by one? Shift the input right by one cell and it becomes zero, zero, two, one, three, zero, and the output is zero, ten, thirteen, nineteen, twelve.

steps.label: KP01 · 25/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: What if we shift by one? Shift the input right by one cell and it becomes zero, zero, two, one, three, zero, and the output is zero, ten, thirteen, nineteen, twelve.

steps.label: KP01 · 25/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: First the top two rows: the blue two, one, three move right by one cell. Then the bottom two rows: the green ten, thirteen, nineteen, twelve also move right by one cell.

steps.label: KP01 · 25/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: Finally the red cell: it is a new value computed at the border, not moved from the old output. The zero at the far right is pushed out of range.

steps.label: KP01 · 26/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Why does it follow? Why is this so? Every output uses the same kernel.

steps.label: KP01 · 26/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Why does it follow? Why is this so? Every output uses the same kernel.

steps.label: KP01 · 26/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: The calculation only looks at the numbers in the window, not at where the window is.

steps.label: KP01 · 26/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: So the same pattern moved anywhere gives the same numbers there. This property is called translation equivariance: however far the input shifts, the output shifts by the same amount.

steps.label: KP01 · 27/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Equivariant = invariant? Translation equivariance is not an unchanged output. When the output does not change at all as the input shifts, it is called translation invariance; a convolutional layer itself does not have this.

steps.label: KP01 · 27/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Equivariant = invariant? Translation equivariance is not an unchanged output. When the output does not change at all as the input shifts, it is called translation invariance; a convolutional layer itself does not have this.

steps.label: KP01 · 27/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Pooling brings only approximate invariance to small shifts, and only locally; the details are in KP08 to KP09.

steps.label: KP01 · 27/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: Equivariance has conditions: the kernel moves one cell at a time, that is a stride of one, and only positions far enough from the border count. In the example above the border cell does not qualify. KP06 discusses this in detail.

steps.label: KP01 · 28/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: A four-part recap! One sentence: a flattened fully connected layer cannot tell who is next to whom and has to learn one weight per connection; a convolutional layer connects only neighbours and shares one kernel over the whole image, so it has far fewer weights, and the feature map follows a shift of the input.

steps.label: KP01 · 28/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: A four-part recap! One sentence: a flattened fully connected layer cannot tell who is next to whom and has to learn one weight per connection; a convolutional layer connects only neighbours and shares one kernel over the whole image, so it has far fewer weights, and the feature map follows a shift of the input.

steps.label: KP01 · 28/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Plain words: instead of letting every output look at the whole image with its own weights, let all outputs use one small kernel, each looking at its own neighbourhood. Looking only nearby means few connections; sharing one kernel means only one set of numbers to learn; wherever the pattern moves, the kernel gives the same numbers there.

steps.label: KP01 · 28/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: Definition and examples: the sliding multiply-add s at i, j is the double sum of I times K, and an image gives a feature map of H minus k plus one by W minus k plus one; at the same size a fully connected layer has H W squared weights and a shared kernel only k squared. Examples: the four by four task 256, 100, 9; the checkerboard feature map five, zero, five; zero, five, zero; five, zero, five; a 1-D input shifted right by one gives an output shifted right by one.

steps.label: KP01 · 29/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Fell for these myths? Misconception one: a flattened MLP surely cannot classify images. This is wrong: it can, only with many weights and hard-to-learn local patterns.

steps.label: KP01 · 29/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Fell for these myths? Misconception one: a flattened MLP surely cannot classify images. This is wrong: it can, only with many weights and hard-to-learn local patterns.

steps.label: KP01 · 29/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Misconception two: a convolutional layer is something new unrelated to fully connected layers. Also wrong: it is a fully connected layer with the two restrictions of sparse connectivity and parameter sharing.

steps.label: KP01 · 29/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: To remember: the two restrictions cut 256 to 100 and then to 9.

steps.label: KP01 · 30/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Two more myths! Misconception three: after sharing weights there are only nine connections. Wrong: there are still one hundred connections, sharing nine numbers.

steps.label: KP01 · 30/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Two more myths! Misconception three: after sharing weights there are only nine connections. Wrong: there are still one hundred connections, sharing nine numbers.

steps.label: KP01 · 30/41 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Misconception four: equivariance means the output does not change. Also wrong: equivariant means the output moves with the input; invariant means it does not move at all, which a convolution itself lacks.

steps.label: KP01 · 30/41 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: To remember: the number of connections and the number of weights are two different numbers; equivariance keeps position and invariance does not.

steps.label: KP01 · 31/41
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Want to go deeper? For a same-size output and a k by k window, the number of neighbour connections is at most H W k squared.

steps.label: KP01 · 31/41 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Want to go deeper? For a same-size output and a k by k window, the number of neighbour connections is at most H W k squared.

steps.label: KP01 · 31/41 (2)
